speaker: Sid
teaser: His hearing aid just died. He's worn them since he was six.
hello: Sid Sprocket, bike mechanic. My left hearing aid died on Tuesday. Seven years old, rest in peace.
I've worn them since I was six. Without them, it's like riding on two flat tyres.

which_ear.say: Same both sides. Always has been, since I was a kid.

say: Since I was tiny. Aids at six, and it hasn't budged in years.
My last test, four years back, matched the one before.
onset.note: Since early childhood; no change in years

ringing.say: None. Quiet as a well-oiled chain.

red_flags.say: No pain, no gunk, no spinning. The only thing broken is the hearing aid.

noise.say: The shop compressor's a beast. Earmuffs on for that, always.
noise.note: Shop compressor; wears earmuffs for it

ear_history.say: No infections, no ops, no knocks. The ear doctor checked me loads as a kid. Nothing to fix, just aids.
ear_history.note: No infections or ops; ear doctor saw him young

family.say: Grandad wore aids from young, and my auntie. We Sprockets say 'pardon?' a lot.
family.note: Grandad and an aunt had early hearing loss

health.say: Fit as a fiddle. I ride to work. No pills, just energy bars.

say: Since I was six! This pair's seven years old.
The left one died Tuesday. The right one's wheezing too.
aids.note: Aids since age 6; this pair is 7 years old

hardest.say: Without aids? Everywhere. With these old ones, the shop radio plus customers is tough.
hardest.note: Old aids struggle with shop noise

right.caption: Sid's RIGHT ear: a roomy, clean canal and a healthy, pearly eardrum.

left.caption: Sid's LEFT ear: the same. Roomy, clean, not a speck of wax.

decision_lines.fit: Fit! Lifelong, steady, matching ears, no red flags. New aids, and his wheels keep turning.
decision_lines.refer: Refer for what? A doctor checked him as a kid. Nothing's changed, ears match, no red flags.
decision_lines.today: Nothing sudden here. His hearing hasn't changed in years. Only his hearing aid died.
decision_lines.clear: No aids needed? A moderate loss in both ears says otherwise. And his old ones just died!

why.prompt: Why is it safe to fit Sid with new hearing aids?
options: The same steady loss in both ears, no gap, no red flags.
Right! Lifelong, unchanged, matching, sensorineural, no red flags. That's a fit.
He has worn hearing aids since he was six.
Old aids aren't a free pass. A sudden change or a red flag still means a doctor.
A loss from childhood never changes.
It can! A sudden drop, or one ear slipping, would send him to a doctor first.
His tympanograms were both type A.
Type A says the eardrums move well. It can't tell you he needs aids.

debrief: Years of aids don't mean skipping the checks. Look, ask and test, every visit.
Bone sat right on air, no gap: that's what shows it's sensorineural. Air alone can't tell.
A new sudden drop: a doctor today. One ear slipping behind: a doctor first. Sid has neither.
goodbye: Whoa! I can hear the freewheel ticking. Crisp as a new chain!
Earmuffs on for that compressor, Sid. Protect the hearing you've got.
The old right one goes in the spares drawer. Every good mechanic keeps spares!

headlines.S: FULL SERVICE FOR SID'S EARS; NEW AIDS FITTED
headlines.A: SID SPROCKET SHIFTS UP A GEAR WITH NEW AIDS
headlines.B: SID FITTED; A FEW STAMPS SLIPPED THEIR CHAIN
headlines.C: SID ROLLS OUT, BUT THE WORKUP HAD A PUNCTURE
headlines.Do-over: SID'S VISIT SENT BACK TO THE WORKSHOP

subheads.S: Lifelong, steady and matching, no red flags: a clean fit after a full check.
subheads.A: Old aids are no shortcut. Look, ask, test, then fit.
subheads.B: The fit was right; a few stamps wandered. Bone on air still proves the type.
subheads.C: Bone tells sensorineural from conductive. Run it whenever air is poorer than 25 dB.
subheads.Do-over: Sid will be back. Bring the otoscope, the questions and the bone buzzer.
